concepts.name: Fundamental Rights: classification, Article 12, Article 13 and Article 14
concepts.description: Part III at a glance, the meaning of State and local authority, laws void under Article 13, and equality before law with its exceptions.
concepts.idea: Article 12 defines State widely and Article 13 voids laws that conflict with Part III; Article 14 joins equality before law with equal protection and has a few constitutional exceptions.
concepts.rule: Part III covers Articles 12 to 35 and began with seven rights; the 44th Amendment, 1978 moved property to Article 300-A, leaving six. Article 12 includes governments and legislatures, local authorities and other authorities. Article 13 voids inconsistent laws; 'law' covers ordinances, delegated legislation and custom, and Kesavananda allows basic-structure review of amendments. Article 14 combines British equality before law (negative) with American equal protection (positive) and allows reasonable classification. Exceptions: Article 31-C, Articles 361, 361-A, 105, 194, foreign diplomats, and Article 359 in an Emergency.
concepts.example: A Governor cannot be arrested during tenure, yet a company can challenge a bye-law as void under Article 13.

questions.q: The right to property was once among the Fundamental Rights. Which of the following correctly states how and where it was moved?
questions.a: 44th Amendment Act, 1978; Article 300-A in Part XII
o: 44th Amendment Act, 1978; Article 300-A in Part XII
42nd Amendment Act, 1976; Article 300-A in Part XII, placed alongside the other legal rights outside Part III
44th Amendment Act, 1978; Article 31-A in Part III, retained there as a limited Fundamental Right
25th Amendment Act, 1971; Article 31-C in Part III, with the right confined to movable property
questions.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed Article 31; the right became a legal and constitutional right under Article 300-A in Part XII, leaving six Fundamental Rights.
w: The 42nd Amendment (1976) did not delete the right; the deletion came two years later, in 1978.
Article 31-A saves laws on acquisition of estates inside Part III; the property right was placed in Article 300-A, Part XII.
The 25th Amendment inserted Article 31-C; it did not remove the right, and the right now sits outside Part III.

questions.q: For the purposes of Article 12, which of the following bodies would qualify as a 'local authority'?
questions.a: A district board (Zilla Parishad) created by statute, holding taxing powers and public duties in a local area
o: A district board (Zilla Parishad) created by statute, holding taxing powers and public duties in a local area
A residents' welfare society registered under the Societies Registration Act that collects maintenance fees from its members
An advisory committee of villagers set up by a government resolution, with no statutory powers or taxing power
A pilgrimage trust created by a private deed and funded by voluntary donations from devotees
questions.e: A local authority is a body of local self-government created by law, with statutory powers, a power to levy taxes or fees and public duties; district boards or Zilla Parishads are listed.
w: A private society is not a body of local self-government created by law; it has no statutory powers or public duties.
A committee set up by resolution lacks statutory powers and the power to levy taxes or fees, which a local authority needs.
A private trust is not created by law for local self-government and has no taxing power.

questions.q: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court's position on a constitutional amendment, read with Article 13, was that an amendment
questions.a: is not 'law' under Article 13, yet can be declared void if it violates a Fundamental Right forming part of the basic structure
o: is not 'law' under Article 13, yet can be declared void if it violates a Fundamental Right forming part of the basic structure
is 'law' under Article 13 and is void if it takes away or abridges any Fundamental Right, whatever the status of that right in the scheme of the Constitution
is beyond judicial review so long as it follows the special procedure laid down in Article 368, including ratification by the States where that is required
is 'law' under Article 13 only when it has been ratified by the legislatures of half of the States, because ratification turns it into ordinary law
questions.e: Article 13 treats an amendment as not 'law', but Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held it can be challenged and voided if it violates a Fundamental Right that is part of the basic structure. Clause 13(4), which excludes amendments from 'law', came later through the 24th Amendment (1971), so the question is worded around the case.
w: That was the earlier Golaknath view; Kesavananda held an amendment is not 'law' and is tested only against the basic structure.
Kesavananda allows review: an amendment violating a basic-structure right can be struck down even if Article 368 was followed.
Ratification by States has nothing to do with whether an amendment is 'law' under Article 13.

questions.q: Article 14 combines two ideas that differ in origin and character. Which pairing is correct?
questions.a: Equal protection of the laws: borrowed from the US Constitution; a positive concept permitting reasonable classification
o: Equal protection of the laws: borrowed from the US Constitution; a positive concept permitting reasonable classification
Equality before law: borrowed from the US Constitution; a positive concept permitting reasonable classification and affirmative action
Equal protection of the laws: taken from British common law; a negative concept denying special privileges to anyone
Equality before law: taken from British common law; a positive concept requiring like persons to be treated alike
questions.e: Equality before law is British in origin, a negative concept and the base of Dicey's Rule of Law; equal protection of the laws is American, a positive concept allowing reasonable classification.
w: Equality before law is the British idea and is the negative limb; the US idea is equal protection.
Equal protection is the American, positive limb; the British, negative one is equality before law.
Equality before law is the British idea but is negative (no special privileges), while 'like treated alike' belongs to equal protection.

questions.q: During a national Emergency, the President may suspend the right to move courts for enforcing Fundamental Rights under Article 359. Which statement about Article 14 and the other rights is correct?
questions.a: Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable, while the right to move courts for Article 14 can be suspended
o: Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable, while the right to move courts for Article 14 can be suspended
Only Article 20 remains enforceable, because Articles 14 and 21 can both be suspended under Article 359
Article 14 remains enforceable, because the equality guarantee cannot be suspended in any kind of Emergency
Articles 14 and 21 remain enforceable, while the right to move courts for Article 20 can be suspended
questions.e: Under Article 359 the enforcement of Fundamental Rights other than Articles 20 and 21 can be suspended in an Emergency, so Article 14 cannot then be enforced in court.
w: Article 21 is also outside the scope of suspension, so Article 20 is not the only survivor.
Article 14 is not protected from suspension; the exceptions are Articles 20 and 21.
Article 20 is one of the two protected rights and cannot be suspended.

1. The Fundamental Rights are called fundamental because the courts guarantee and enforce them.
2. A person must first approach the High Court under Article 226 before the Supreme Court can be moved under Article 32 for a Fundamental Right.
3. Part III is described as the Conscience of the Constitution, and Parts III and IV together as the Magna Carta of India.
4. The Constitution as originally framed contained seven Fundamental Rights.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: The Fundamental Rights are called fundamental because the courts guarantee and enforce them. Statement 2 is incorrect: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, so a person may go directly to the Supreme Court. Statement 3 is incorrect: The labels are swapped: Part III is the Magna Carta, and Parts III and IV together are the Conscience of the Constitution. Statement 4 is correct: Seven, including the right to property.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 13:

1. Article 13 makes the Fundamental Rights enforceable protections rather than mere ideals by voiding conflicting laws.
2. Laws in force before 26 January 1950, including British and princely-state laws, become void in their entirety under clause 13(1).
3. Clause 13(2) bars the State from making a law that violates Fundamental Rights, and such a law is void.
4. Clause 13(3) defines law broadly so that no form of legal authority escapes judicial review.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Article 13 makes the Fundamental Rights enforceable protections rather than mere ideals by voiding conflicting laws. Statement 2 is incorrect: They are void only to the extent of the inconsistency. Statement 3 is correct: Clause 13(2) bars the State from making a law that violates Fundamental Rights, and such a law is void. Statement 4 is correct: Clause 13(3) defines law broadly so that no form of legal authority escapes judicial review.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Fundamental Rights in an Emergency:

1. The six freedoms of Article 19 are suspended automatically when a national Emergency is declared on the ground of armed rebellion.
2. Neither Article 20 nor Article 21 can be suspended while a national Emergency is in force.
3. Suspending the right to move courts under Article 359 needs a constitutional amendment passed by Parliament.
4. A Presidential order under Article 359 cannot suspend Article 14, which is protected in the same way as Articles 20 and 21.

Statement 2 is correct: Neither Article 20 nor Article 21 can be suspended while a national Emergency is in force. Statement 3 is incorrect: It is done by a Presidential order. questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: A law may lawfully treat one reasonably defined class of persons differently from another under Article 14.
Statement-II: Under equal protection of the laws, persons placed in like circumstances must be treated alike in the privileges conferred and liabilities imposed.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct: Article 14 permits reasonable classification, so one reasonably defined class may lawfully be treated differently from another. Statement-II is correct: equal protection of the laws means that persons placed in like circumstances must be treated alike in the privileges conferred and liabilities imposed. Because the test is likeness of circumstances, a reasonable difference in circumstances can justify different treatment, so II explains I.
w: Statement-II does give the reason for Statement-I: the test is likeness of circumstances, so a reasonable difference in circumstances can justify different treatment.
Statement-II is correct, not incorrect: equal protection requires like treatment of persons in like circumstances.
Statement-I is correct, not incorrect: Article 14 permits reasonable classification.

concepts.name: Articles 15 and 16(1)-(3), (5): non-discrimination, reservation judgments and EWS
concepts.description: Article 15 clauses, the reservation judgments from Champakam to Janhit Abhiyan, EWS criteria and the opening clauses of Article 16.
concepts.idea: Article 15 bars discrimination and permits special provisions, while the reservation case law shaped the 50 percent ceiling and the EWS quota.
concepts.rule: Article 15(1) binds the State and 15(2) also private persons. Clauses 15(3), 15(4), 15(5) and 15(6) permit special provision for women and children, backward classes, admissions (93rd Amendment) and EWS (103rd Amendment). Champakam led to the 1st Amendment; Balaji set the 50 percent cap; Indra Sawhney upheld the 27 percent OBC quota with the creamy layer. EWS needs income below Rs 8 lakh and fails the asset tests. Article 16(1)-(3) and (5) cover equality of opportunity, the grounds, residence and religious offices.
concepts.example: A family with Rs 7 lakh income and 5 acres of land is excluded from the EWS quota.

questions.q: The decision in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan and its sequel are best described by which of the following?
questions.a: Caste-based allocation of educational seats was struck down as violating the equality and non-discrimination guarantees, and the 1st Amendment (1951) then inserted Article 15(4)
o: Caste-based allocation of educational seats was struck down as violating the equality and non-discrimination guarantees, and the 1st Amendment (1951) then inserted Article 15(4)
The ruling striking down caste quotas in college seats led to the 93rd Amendment of 2005, which inserted Article 15(5) to cover admissions
The M.R. Balaji ruling of 1950 on caste-based college seats led to the 1st Amendment of 1951, which inserted Article 15(4)
The Devadasan ruling of 1950 on caste-based college seats led to the 1st Amendment of 1951, which inserted Article 15(4)
questions.e: Champakam Dorairajan struck down the caste-based allocation of seats as violating the Constitution's equality and non-discrimination guarantees; the 1st Amendment, 1951 then inserted Article 15(4).
w: Article 15(5) came in 2005 after Inamdar, not as a sequel to Champakam.
Balaji (on the 50 percent cap) came later, in 1962; the 1st Amendment answered Champakam.
Devadasan (1964) dealt with carry-forward rules in jobs, long after the 1st Amendment.

questions.q: Under the 2019 criteria for the 10 percent EWS quota, which of the following families would still be eligible?
questions.a: Gross annual income of Rs 7.5 lakh from all sources, 3 acres of agricultural land and an 800 sq ft flat
o: Gross annual income of Rs 7.5 lakh from all sources, 3 acres of agricultural land and an 800 sq ft flat
Gross annual income of Rs 7 lakh from salary and farming, with 5 acres of agricultural land owned by the family
Gross annual income of Rs 6 lakh from all sources, with a residential flat of 1100 sq ft in a city
Gross annual income of Rs 5 lakh from business, with a residential plot of 250 sq yards in a non-notified area
questions.e: Income must be below Rs 8 lakh, but 5 acres or more, a flat of 1000 sq ft or more, or a plot of 100 sq yards (notified municipality) or 200 sq yards (elsewhere) excludes the family.
w: Holding 5 acres or more of agricultural land excludes a family irrespective of income.
A flat of 1000 sq ft or more excludes a family regardless of income.
In areas outside notified municipalities a plot of 200 sq yards or more excludes the family.

questions.q: In Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022), the Supreme Court by a 3-2 majority
questions.a: upheld the 10 percent EWS quota, holding that the 50 percent ceiling is not inviolable and that excluding SC, ST and OBC from it is valid
o: upheld the 10 percent EWS quota, holding that the 50 percent ceiling is not inviolable and that excluding SC, ST and OBC from it is valid
struck down the 103rd Amendment because crossing the 50 percent ceiling breached the basic structure of the Constitution, voiding the EWS quota
upheld the EWS quota but held that SC, ST and OBC families must also be eligible to claim it, since excluding them breached equality
upheld the 103rd Amendment but struck down its exclusion of SC, ST and OBC families from the EWS quota as discriminatory
questions.e: The 3-2 majority upheld Article 15(6), the 10 percent EWS quota, the exclusion of SC, ST and OBC from it, and held the 50 percent rule not inviolable.
w: The majority held the 50 percent rule is not inviolable, so no breach of basic structure was found.
The majority upheld the exclusion of those groups from the EWS quota.
The exclusion was upheld by the majority, not struck down.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes Article 15(2) from Article 15(1)?
questions.a: It restrains private individuals as well as the State from denying access to shops, hotels and public places
o: It restrains private individuals as well as the State from denying access to shops, hotels and public places
It protects non-citizens as well as citizens against discrimination in access to public places and State-run facilities
It also prohibits discrimination on grounds of descent and residence in public places, facilities and services
It covers only wells, tanks and roads maintained wholly out of State funds, not shops or hotels
questions.e: Article 15(1) restrains only the State, while Article 15(2) binds the State and private persons in access to shops, restaurants, hotels, entertainment places, wells, tanks, ghats and roads.
w: Both clauses speak of 'any citizen'; the difference is the persons bound, not the persons protected.
Descent and residence are added in Article 16(2), not Article 15(2).
Article 15(2) covers facilities maintained wholly or partly from State funds or dedicated to public use, plus shops and hotels.

questions.q: Article 16(3) of the Constitution allows
questions.a: Parliament to prescribe a residence requirement for employment under a State or Union Territory, or a local authority there
o: Parliament to prescribe a residence requirement for employment under a State or Union Territory, or a local authority there
each State legislature to prescribe a residence requirement for employment under that State, independently of Parliament
the President to prescribe a residence requirement for employment under the Central Government, by notification, without any law of Parliament
Parliament to prescribe a residence requirement only for services of Union Territories, not for the States or any authority within them
questions.e: Article 16(3) empowers Parliament to prescribe residence as a requirement; the 1957 Act expired in 1974, leaving only Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
w: The power belongs to Parliament, not to State legislatures.
Article 16(3) concerns employment under a State or Union Territory and is exercised by Parliament, not the President.
The clause covers State employment as well as Union Territories and local authorities.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 15:

1. The State is barred by Article 15(1) from adverse distinctions against citizens made solely on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
2. Article 15(3) allows the State to make special provisions for women and children.
3. Article 15(4) allows special provision for backward classes, SCs and STs and also overrides Article 29(2).
4. Article 15(2) restrains only the State, not private individuals, in access to shops, restaurants and hotels.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: The State is barred by Article 15(1) from adverse distinctions against citizens made solely on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Statement 2 is correct: Article 15(3) allows the State to make special provisions for women and children. Statement 3 is correct: Article 15(4) allows special provision for backward classes, SCs and STs and also overrides Article 29(2). Statement 4 is incorrect: Article 15(2) binds the State and private individuals.

'1 and 2 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct
'2 and 3 only' leaves out statement 1, which is correct

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about reservation judgments up to 1992:

1. M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore laid down a 50 percent cap and required backwardness to be social as well as educational.
2. Devadasan v. Union of India held that the carry-forward rule may take total reservation beyond the 50 percent ceiling.

concepts.rule: Article 16(4) covers backward classes, with 16(4A) (77th, 1995) for promotions, 16(4B) (81st, 2000) for carry-forward vacancies and 16(6) (103rd, 2019) for EWS. questions.q: Article 16(4) of the Constitution enables the State to reserve appointments or posts for

o: any backward class which, in the State's opinion, is not adequately represented in the services, a category that includes OBCs
only the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, since OBC reservation rests on a separate clause of Article 16 of its own, which the State must invoke instead
any economically weaker class of citizens, whether or not it is inadequately represented in the State services, on the basis of income alone
any class which, in the opinion of Parliament, is not adequately represented in the Central services of the Union, and not in the State services at all
questions.e: Article 16(4) uses the words 'backward class not adequately represented in the State's opinion'; Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld the 27 percent OBC quota under it. The view that only SC/ST are covered by Article 16(4) is therefore wrong.

w: Article 18(1) bans every title other than military or academic ones, whether conferred on a citizen or a foreigner.
Article 18(2) forbids a citizen from accepting any title from a foreign State; consent is relevant only for office-holders' gifts and titles to non-citizens.

concepts.name: Article 22 ordinary arrest, Articles 23-26

concepts.rule: Four Part I rights of Article 22: grounds, lawyer, production within 24 hours excluding travel, release unless the Magistrate authorises.
